title: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown
goal: By the end you can set up a pool you can debug at 3 a.m.: named threads, every failure reported with its request id, context carried to the worker, the right metrics, a clean shutdown, and no task waiting on another task in the same pool.

warmup.q: A month-end statement job runs on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Each merchant's task submits a ledger query to the same pool and calls `get()` on it. With 5 merchants it takes 2 seconds. With 400 merchants, what happens?
options: It takes about 80 times longer, because the pool is busy
The pool grows past 20 threads to keep up
It hangs forever with the CPU near zero
The JVM detects the deadlock and throws in one of the tasks
warmup.why: The first 20 merchant tasks take every thread, and each one waits for a query that is queued behind 380 other merchant tasks. No thread will ever be free to run a query, so the job hangs. A fixed pool never grows, and the JVM's deadlock detector looks for cycles of locks, not tasks waiting on queued tasks, so nothing throws.

sections.h: Name your threads, and know where failures go
sections.body:
The default names are `pool-3-thread-7`. In a thread dump of a service with eight pools, that tells you nothing. Name them, and the name shows up in every log line that prints the thread, in every thread dump and in every profiler:

```java
ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory();   // JDK 21+: ledger-0, ledger-1, ...
ExecutorService ledgerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, named);
```

```kotlin
val named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()            // JDK 21+: ledger-0, ledger-1, ...
val ledgerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, named)
```

Before JDK 21 you write a small `ThreadFactory` with an `AtomicInteger`, or use Guava's `ThreadFactoryBuilder`.

Now failures. Lesson 1 of this track showed that `execute` and `submit` treat an exception differently, and in production the difference decides whether you ever hear about it.

With `execute`, the exception escapes the task. The worker thread dies, its `UncaughtExceptionHandler` runs, and the pool starts a new thread in its place. The default handler prints a stack trace to `System.err`, outside your logging framework and its request ids.

With `submit`, the `FutureTask` catches the exception and keeps it. Nothing is printed. If nobody calls `get()`, which is normal for fire-and-forget work, the failure is gone.

So an `UncaughtExceptionHandler` on the thread factory covers only half the cases. To cover both, catch failures in one place that every task passes through. `submit`, `invokeAll` and `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, pool)` all end up in `execute`, so a `ThreadPoolExecutor` subclass that overrides `execute` and wraps each task sees everything. Report the failure there, with the request id, and don't rethrow: rethrowing only kills the worker and prints the same stack trace a second time. The lab builds exactly that pool.

sections.h: Watch the queue, the active count, rejections and time in queue
sections.body:
A pool is a queue in front of a few threads, and it is the first place a slow dependency shows up. Four numbers tell you most of what you need.

The queue size, `getQueue().size()`. A queue that keeps growing means tasks arrive faster than they finish. Little's law from lesson 3 of this track says the wait grows with it.

The active count, `getActiveCount()`, compared with the maximum. A pool pinned at its maximum for minutes is saturated, and it's usually waiting on something downstream rather than working.

Rejections. `ThreadPoolExecutor` doesn't count them for you. Wrap the `RejectedExecutionHandler` in one that increments a counter and then throws, as `MetricsDemo` does. Every rejection is a request you turned away, so alert on it.

Time in queue. This is latency the caller feels and the task never measures. Record the time when a task is submitted, in the same wrapper that carries the context, and compare it when the task starts.

The getters are approximate. The Javadoc says so, because the threads keep changing them while you read. That's fine for a dashboard and wrong for program logic. Micrometer's `ExecutorServiceMetrics` binds most of these numbers for you.

Of the four, queue time and rejections are what your customers feel. A pool with an empty queue and no rejections is healthy, however busy its threads look.

sections.h: Pool-induced deadlock: tasks that wait for tasks in the same pool
sections.body:
Here is a statement job that works in every test:

```java
pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> ledger.lines(merchant));   // a task inside a task
    return render(merchant, lines.get());                                     // waits for it
});
```

```kotlin
pool.submit<String> {
    val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { ledger.lines(merchant) }   // a task inside a task
    render(merchant, lines.get())                                     // waits for it
}
```

With 20 threads and 5 merchants, it's fine. At month-end it gets 400 merchants. The first 20 statement tasks take all 20 threads. Each one submits its fetch, and the fetches join the back of the queue, behind 380 statement tasks. Every thread now waits for a task that can only run on a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. The CPU drops to zero. Nothing throws. A thread dump shows no "deadlock found" line, because no lock is involved: every thread is just `WAITING` in `FutureTask.get`. *Java Concurrency in Practice* calls this thread starvation deadlock.

Three fixes, in the order I'd try them:

1. Don't block inside the pool. Compose: `supplyAsync(() -> ledger.lines(m), pool).thenApply(lines -> render(m, lines))`. The render step runs as a callback when the fetch completes, so no thread waits. Only the caller joins at the end.
2. Don't split what doesn't need splitting. If the statement task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline in the same task.
3. Give each stage its own pool. Statement tasks may wait for a separate fetch pool, as long as fetch tasks never wait for the statement pool. That's a bulkhead from lesson 3.

A cached pool with no thread limit also makes the hang go away, by starting a thread for every waiting task. That moves the problem to memory and to the database connection pool. `join()` inside a `CompletableFuture` stage is the same bug, which is why lesson 6 of this track warned against it.

sections.h: Shut down in order, with a deadline

analogy: Running pools in production is like running a busy restaurant kitchen. Name tags on every cook (thread names) let you see who is stuck. An order ticket travels with each dish (the request context), and every cook throws the old ticket away before taking the next one. The board by the pass shows how many tickets are waiting (queue size) and how many customers were turned away (rejections). The deadlock is two cooks who each started a dish that needs a sauce, put the sauce order at the back of the queue, and stand waiting for it, while nobody is left to make sauce. The analogy breaks at closing time: a kitchen can tell customers to leave. A pool has to stop its own intake first, then let each station finish in order, and it gets one fixed deadline from the orchestrator.
in_your_world: In a payment service, a named pool per dependency (`issuer-`, `ledger-`, `fraud-`) turns a thread dump during an incident into a map: 40 `issuer-` threads in a socket read means the issuer is slow, not your code. Put the request id or idempotency key in the MDC at the edge, and make every pool carry it, so a ledger write logged on `ledger-7` can be traced back to the authorization that caused it. Count rejections on the authorization pool and alert on them, because each one is a declined payment. Settlement and statement jobs are where pool-induced deadlock likes to live: nested fan-outs on one shared pool that only hang at month-end volume. On shutdown, pause the Kafka consumer before draining the pools, so no offset is committed for work that never ran, and remember that a Temporal worker factory needs its own shutdown call, so activities in flight can finish.
mistake: The most common mistake is fire-and-forget with `submit`: `pool.submit(() -> audit.write(event))` with nobody keeping the `Future`. The audit write starts failing on a schema change, every exception sits in a `Future` that is garbage the moment it's created, and nothing is logged for days. People use `submit` because it's the method they know, and the failure path never runs in tests. Use `execute` for fire-and-forget work, or better, run every pool through a wrapper that reports failures from both `execute` and `submit` with the request id, the way the lab's `ProductionPool` does.

compare.title: Carrying the MDC: an executor wrapper vs a coroutine context element

java.title: MdcExecutor.java (SLF4J)

kotlin.title: MdcCoroutine.kt (kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j)

compare.note: The Java wrapper installs the context once, because a task stays on one thread from start to finish. A coroutine can move to another thread at every suspension point, so a wrapper around the whole coroutine wouldn't be enough. `MDCContext()` and `asContextElement` are thread context elements: the dispatcher installs the value each time the coroutine resumes on a thread and restores the thread's old value when it suspends. One trap: an `MDC.put` inside the coroutine is lost at the next suspension, because the element keeps reinstalling the map it captured. The kotlinx docs say to wrap the change in `withContext(MDCContext())`.

worked.title: Diagnose a statement job that stopped at month-end

steps.say: The month-end statement job has produced nothing for 30 minutes. CPU on the pod is near zero. A thread dump (`jcmd <pid> Thread.print`) shows all 20 `stmt-` threads in the same place. Before reading on, say what they are waiting for.
steps.code:
"stmt-3" #41 prio=5 os_prio=0 ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
	- parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(...)
	at com.acme.settlement.StatementJob.lambda$run$0(StatementJob.java)
	...

steps.say: Every thread is inside a statement task, parked in `FutureTask.get()`, waiting for another task's result. The pool's metrics finish the story: `active=20`, the queue at 380 and not moving, `completed` flat. The awaited fetch tasks are in that queue, behind the other statement tasks, and they need a free thread that will never come. The dump has no "Found one Java-level deadlock" line, because the detector looks for cycles of locks, and a `Future` has no owner.
The fix is to stop holding a thread while waiting. Compose the fetch and the render, start every merchant's pipeline, and let only the job's own thread wait at the end.
steps.code:
List<CompletableFuture<String>> statements = merchants.stream()
        .map(m -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> ledger.lines(m), pool)   // 1. fetch on the pool
                .thenApply(lines -> render(m, lines)))                       // 2. render as a callback
        .toList();
return statements.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();           // 3. only the caller waits
steps.alt_code:
val statements = merchants.map { m ->
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ ledger.lines(m) }, pool)                // 1. fetch on the pool
        .thenApply { lines -> render(m, lines) }                           // 2. render as a callback
}
return statements.map { it.join() }                                        // 3. only the caller waits

steps.say: Then make the next incident shorter. The `stmt-` names already paid off: they showed at once which pool was stuck. Add a dashboard panel and an alert for the queue size and the oldest task's wait on this pool, so a queue that stops moving pages someone within minutes, not after the merchants complain.

lab.title: A production pool, and a deadlock to fix
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The two `StatementJob` tests time out after 5 seconds: that is the deadlock.
Write `ProductionPool.create`: build the factory with `Thread.ofPlatform().name(name + "-", 0).factory()` and pass it to the private constructor, which already sets up the bounded queue.

Write `ProductionPool.execute`. Read `RequestContext.get()` first, on the calling thread. Then call `super.execute` with a lambda that saves the worker's own context, sets the captured id, runs the task, and restores the saved context in a `finally`.

Report failures inside that lambda: catch `RuntimeException | Error` from `task.run()` and report it without rethrowing. After `run()` returns, if the task is a `Future` whose `state()` is `FAILED`, report `exceptionNow()`.
Fix `StatementJob.run`: start a `supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render)` pipeline for every merchant, then join them all on the calling thread.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: Capture the id before `super.execute`. Inside the lambda you are already on the worker, where `RequestContext.get()` returns the worker's value.
`task instanceof Future<?> f && f.state() == Future.State.FAILED` (JDK 19+), then `f.exceptionNow()`, gives you the original exception, not an `ExecutionException`.
If `reportsExecuteFailures` sees the next task on `ledger-1`, your wrapper rethrew: the worker died and the pool replaced it.
The `StatementJob` fix needs no second pool. A `thenApply` callback never holds a thread while it waits.

drill.title: A context-carrying executor from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `Executor withRequestId(Executor delegate)`: every task runs with the `RequestContext` of the thread that called `execute`, and the worker's own value is restored afterwards. Then compare. Where did you read the context, and is the restore in a `finally`?

answer.title: Contexts.java

alt.title: Contexts.kt

recap: Name every pool's threads (`Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()` on JDK 21+), so dumps and logs say which pool is stuck.
An `UncaughtExceptionHandler` only sees `execute` failures; `submit` hides them in the `Future`. Wrap `execute` once to report both, with the request id.
ThreadLocal context (MDC, tracing, security) doesn't follow a task to a pool. Capture it at submission, install it in the worker, restore it in `finally`.
Watch queue size, active count against the maximum, rejections and time in queue. Count rejections yourself in the handler.
A task that blocks on another task in the same bounded pool can hang the pool forever. Compose instead, do the work inline, or give each stage its own pool.
Shut down in order: stop intake, then pools upstream first, all within one deadline inside the grace period; log what `shutdownNow` returns.

quiz.q: A report service uses a fixed pool of 4. Each report task submits two sub-queries to the same pool and calls `get()` on both. It passes every test and hangs at month-end with the CPU near zero. What happened?
options: The sub-queries got slow, so the reports need more time
Four report tasks hold all four threads, and each waits for sub-queries queued behind other reports, so nothing can ever finish
Two report tasks locked each other's monitors
The queue overflowed and the sub-queries were rejected
quiz.why: This is pool-induced deadlock. The awaited tasks need a free thread, and all the threads are busy waiting for them. Slowness wouldn't drop the CPU to zero forever, no monitors are involved, and a fixed pool's queue is unbounded, so nothing is rejected.

quiz.q: A request thread puts `requestId=req-42` in the MDC and submits a task to a fixed pool. The task logs a line. With no context propagation in place, which request id is on that line?
options: `req-42`, because pool threads inherit the MDC
None, every time, because pool threads clear their MDC between tasks
Whatever that pool thread last had: often none, sometimes a stale id from an earlier task
The logging call throws, because the MDC isn't thread-safe
quiz.why: The MDC is a `ThreadLocal` on the worker thread. That thread was created long ago and is reused, so it holds nothing, or whatever an earlier task put there and didn't clean up. Nothing clears it between tasks unless your wrapper does.

quiz.q: Which number warns you first that a bounded `ThreadPoolExecutor` is falling behind, before it starts rejecting?
options: `getPoolSize()`
`getCompletedTaskCount()`
`getLargestPoolSize()`
`getQueue().size()` climbing, or the time tasks spend in the queue
quiz.why: A queue that keeps growing means arrivals outpace completions, and every queued task's wait grows with it. Pool size is fixed in a fixed pool, the completed count only rises, and the largest pool size is history. When the queue is full, rejections start.

quiz.q: Intake hands work to `enrichPool`, whose tasks submit to `ledgerPool`. The pod gets `SIGTERM`. In what order do you shut down?
options: Stop intake, shut down `enrichPool` and wait for it, then shut down `ledgerPool` and wait for it
Shut down `ledgerPool`, then `enrichPool`, then stop intake
Call `shutdownNow()` on both pools at once to be quick
Stop intake, then shut down `ledgerPool` first because it holds the money
quiz.why: Upstream first. While `enrichPool` drains, its tasks still submit to `ledgerPool`, so `ledgerPool` must keep accepting work until then. Shutting it down first makes those submissions fail with `RejectedExecutionException`, and `shutdownNow` on both interrupts work that could have finished.

quiz.q: From "Inside ThreadPoolExecutor": a `ProductionPool` has 4 threads and a queue of 100, with the default `AbortPolicy`. 200 slow tasks arrive at once. How many are rejected?
quiz.why: Four tasks start the four threads, the next 100 fill the queue, and core equals max, so the pool can't grow. The remaining 96 are rejected with `RejectedExecutionException`, which is what a bounded queue is for: the caller hears about the overload at once.

flashcards.front: How do you name pool threads on JDK 21+?
flashcards.back: Pass `Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()` to the executor. Threads are named ledger-0, ledger-1, ...
Only tasks run with `execute()`. With `submit()` the exception is stored in the Future and nothing is printed.

flashcards.front: Why does an MDC value disappear when you hand a task to a pool?
flashcards.back: The MDC is a ThreadLocal, and the task runs on another thread. Capture it at submission and install it in the worker.

flashcards.front: Why must a context wrapper restore the worker's value in `finally`?
flashcards.back: Pool threads are reused. Whatever one task leaves behind is the next task's context.
Tasks in a bounded pool block waiting for other tasks queued in the same pool; every thread waits and the awaited tasks never start.

flashcards.front: Name two fixes for pool-induced deadlock.
flashcards.back: Compose instead of blocking (`supplyAsync(...).thenApply(...)`), or give each stage its own pool so waits never point back into the same pool.

flashcards.front: In what order do you shut down chained pools?
flashcards.back: Stop intake, then shut down the upstream pool and wait, then the downstream one, all within one deadline.

terms.plain: The object a pool asks for new threads; it sets their names, daemon flag and exception handler.
Code that runs when an exception escapes a thread's run method.
Mapped Diagnostic Context: per-thread key-value pairs that SLF4J adds to every log line.
Copying thread-local state such as a request id from the submitting thread to the worker.
Every thread in a pool waits for a task that is queued in that same pool. Also called thread starvation deadlock.
Stopping intake, letting in-flight work finish within a deadline, and recording what didn't.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's statement job works with 5 merchants and hangs with 400, on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Explain what is happening and two ways to fix it.
explain_back.answer: Each merchant task submits its ledger fetch to the same pool and blocks on `get()`. With 400 merchants, the first 20 tasks take every thread, and their fetches are queued behind the other 380 merchant tasks. A fetch can only run on a free thread, and every thread is waiting for a fetch, so nothing ever finishes. The CPU is idle and nothing throws, because no lock is involved. One fix is to stop blocking inside the pool: start `supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render)` for each merchant, so rendering is a callback and only the job's own thread waits at the end. Another is to run the fetches on a separate pool, so the statement threads wait on a pool that never waits back on them. Simplest of all, if the statement task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline.
